packages.title: Mutual gravitational interaction
packages.lesson: Choose the pair as a system. Mutual Newtonian forces have equal magnitude and opposite directions: F=Gm₁m₂/r². For isolated bodies, a₁=F/m₁ and a₂=F/m₂. From initial rest, impulses are opposite, so p₁+p₂=0. A heavier mass does not exert a larger mutual force.

examples.prompt: A 2 kg and 6 kg body interact with a 12 N mutual force. Find acceleration magnitudes.
examples.solution: a₂kg=6 m/s²; a₆kg=2 m/s². The forces are equal.

examples.prompt: An isolated 3 kg body has speed 4 m/s after release with a 12 kg partner. Find partner velocity.
examples.solution: Choose the first body's direction positive. p=12 kg·m/s, so partner velocity −1 m/s.

examples.prompt: Two isolated masses are initially at rest. One moves 3 m while the other moves 1 m toward it. Find their mass ratio.

packages.condition: Only mutual force for the pair; compare accelerations in an inertial frame. Distances between spherical bodies are center-to-center.
packages.misconception: Equal forces do not imply equal accelerations or speeds.

tasks.prediction: Can different measured accelerations arise from equal forces?
tasks.prompt: Two isolated bodies A and B start at rest. At one instant their acceleration magnitudes are 0.6 and 0.2 m/s². B has mass 9 kg. Later A has moved 8 cm toward B; determine A's mass and B's displacement. State why the separation decreases by a different amount.

tasks.prediction: Does equal acceleration prove equal gravitational forces?
tasks.prompt: Two equal-mass bodies attract one another. An additional external force of magnitude F acts on the left body toward the right, where F is the mutual gravitational force magnitude at that instant. Compare accelerations, total external force and the COM acceleration. Evaluate the claim that unequal accelerations disprove Newton's third law.

packages.title: Planetary gravity scaling
packages.lesson: For a spherical body, g=GM/R². With mean density ρ, M=(4π/3)ρR³, so g=(4πG/3)ρR. Compare ratios only after deciding which quantities are held constant. Weight W=mg, mass is intrinsic.

examples.prompt: Same mass, twice radius: find gravity ratio.
Same mean density, triple radius: compare gravity and mass.
A planet has 8 times Earth's mass and 2 times its radius. Compare weight and density.
examples.solution: g/g_E=2; same object's weight doubles; density ratio=8/8=1.

packages.condition: Spherical bodies, surface field, negligible rotation; density is mean density. No assumption of uniform internal density needed for exterior field.
packages.misconception: Do not vary M and R independently when density is constrained.

tasks.prediction: Can a smaller planet have greater surface gravity?
tasks.prompt: A spherical planet B has surface gravity 3/2 that of A and mean density 3 times A. Determine its radius and mass ratios, then compare weights of the same 2 kg probe.

tasks.prediction: Can mass and radius be inferred uniquely from two gravity readings?
tasks.prompt: An unknown spherical planet has surface gravity g₀. At height h above its surface, the measured gravity is g₀/4. h is a known positive length. Prove that its radius and mass are uniquely determined. Explain what becomes ambiguous if the height is unknown.

packages.title: Free fall and apparent weight
packages.lesson: Weight mg is gravitational force; apparent weight is a contact force. For a body on a scale in an elevator, take up positive: N−mg=ma. During free fall a=−g, N=0. For a supported body on a string use T instead of N. A string cannot exert compression.

examples.prompt: A 5 kg body in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s²; g=10. Find scale reading.
Same body, lift accelerates downward at 4 m/s².
examples.solution: N=5(10−4)=30 N; velocity direction is irrelevant.

examples.prompt: Two masses hang from a support released into free fall.
examples.solution: All accelerate at g in the ideal model; tension/contact readings vanish if no other constraints act.

packages.condition: Uniform near-surface g, no air resistance, ideal constraints; contact force cannot be negative.
packages.misconception: Zero scale reading does not mean gravity has vanished.

tasks.prediction: Can a downward-moving lift have a reading greater than mg?
tasks.prompt: A 4 kg person stands on a scale in a lift moving downward. The scale reads 52 N for 3 s, then 20 N for 2 s. Take g=10 m/s²; initial velocity is −8 m/s (up positive). Find velocity at the end and decide whether the person reversed direction.

tasks.prediction: Can an ideal string maintain a negative tension?
tasks.prompt: A 2 kg mass hangs from a ceiling inside a cabin. The cabin is driven downward at 12 m/s² while g=10 m/s². A student predicts T=−4 N and says the string pushes upward. Evaluate the claim and describe the immediate motion relative to the cabin.

packages.title: Inverse vertical-motion modelling
packages.lesson: Use one origin and downward positive. For constant g, H=ut+gt²/2; upward launch has negative initial velocity. Two observations of the same endpoint yield two equations; subtract or eliminate common unknowns. A third independent measurement can determine an otherwise missing absolute scale.

examples.prompt: Drop from rest for 2 s at g=10. Find depth.
Throw upward at 5 m/s, arrive after 3 s; g=10. Find downward displacement.
Same endpoint reached in 2 s with downward speed 5 m/s and 3 s with upward speed 5 m/s; infer g.

packages.condition: Same starting point and endpoint, uniform acceleration, no drag; all times measured from respective releases.
packages.misconception: Different flight times do not imply different depths; signed initial velocities matter.

tasks.prediction: Does a known depth remove the need to know g in advance?
tasks.prompt: A shaft of known depth 45 m is used for two trials. A stone dropped from rest arrives after 3 s; another launched upward arrives after 5 s. Find g and launch speed. Predict the arrival time for a downward launch at the same speed.

tasks.prediction: Can three timing measurements determine an absolute length without any length data?
tasks.prompt: Three releases from the same point to a common lower endpoint are a drop, an upward throw and an equal-speed downward throw. Measured times are 4 s, 8 s and 2 s respectively. Show whether the times are consistent with constant g. Can g, launch speed and depth each be found uniquely? If not, identify a family of solutions.

packages.title: Circular orbital reasoning
packages.lesson: For a small body in a circular orbit around a spherical central mass, gravity supplies the inward acceleration: GMm/r²=mv²/r. Thus v²=GM/r, T=2πr/v. Orbital speed is tangential; radius is measured from center. These are circular orbit relations, not general elliptical formulas.

examples.prompt: A circular radius doubles around the same mass. Compare speed.
A satellite has speed 2 km/s at radius 1000 km. Determine period.
Two circular orbits have speed ratio 3:1 around one star. Compare radii and periods.

packages.condition: Neglect other forces, central mass recoil, drag, and rotation effects. Use center-to-center r.
packages.misconception: Do not treat centripetal force as an additional force or use height as radius.

tasks.prediction: Can a slower circular satellite have a shorter period around the same star?
tasks.prompt: Two satellites circle the same star. One takes 8 times as long per orbit as the other. Its orbital circumference is unknown. Derive radius and speed ratios, and check that the period relation is consistent.

tasks.prediction: Does equal orbital speed imply equal central mass?
tasks.prompt: Two planets orbit different stars in circular orbits. Planet B has twice A's orbital radius and the same orbital speed. Compare central masses and orbital periods. Explain why the same speed does not establish identical gravitational acceleration.

packages.title: Two-body gravitational energy
packages.lesson: Use the pair potential U=−Gm₁m₂/r once. An isolated pair initially at relative rest has equal opposite COM momenta. Finite separation change releases Gm₁m₂(1/r−1/s), shared between both kinetic energies. In a lab with COM speed V, velocities are COM velocities plus V, and total K=K_internal+½(m₁+m₂)V²; the constant translation term cancels in energy differences.

examples.prompt: Two unequal masses m and 2m gain a total 12 J from mutual attraction. Partition kinetic energy.
examples.solution: Equal momentum magnitudes ⇒ K_m/K_2m=2; 8 J and 4 J.

examples.prompt: An isolated pair m and 2m starts at separation s; later r=2s/3. Find total kinetic energy.
In a COM frame masses m and 2m move toward each other at +4 and −2 m/s. A lab boost is +3 m/s. Find lab velocities and compare relative speed.
examples.solution: Lab velocities +7 and +1; relative speed 6 m/s in both. COM kinetic term adds ½(3m)×9, independent of internal motion.

packages.condition: Point masses or nonoverlapping spherical bodies; isolated Newtonian pair, no external work, finite initial separation. Galilean frames only.
packages.misconception: Do not count potential twice or allocate all released energy to one moving mass.

tasks.prediction: Which body receives more kinetic energy?
tasks.prompt: Two isolated point masses m and 3m start from rest at separation s. Later the lighter body has kinetic energy Gm²/s. Determine their separation and the heavier body's kinetic energy.

tasks.prediction: Can a body be momentarily stationary in one frame while its acceleration is nonzero?
tasks.prompt: Two isolated point masses m and 2m initially rest relative to one another at separation s. Their COM travels at constant velocity V along the line of centers. At separation r<s the heavier body is instantaneously stationary in the lab. Taking its COM velocity opposite V, derive V² and refute the claim that gravity on it is zero. Explain the frame independence of potential-energy change.

packages.title: Gravity and electrostatic equilibrium
packages.lesson: For a charged suspended bob in static equilibrium with a horizontal electric force, tension balances both weight and electric force. T cosθ=mg, T sinθ=F_e, so tanθ=F_e/(mg). If F_e depends on separation, solve the geometry and force relation together rather than holding force fixed.

examples.prompt: A 0.2 kg bob experiences 1 N horizontal force; g=10. Find tanθ.
Same horizontal force at half g.
examples.solution: tanθ doubles; θ itself does not necessarily double.

packages.condition: Static equilibrium, ideal string; horizontal force must be specified; original 2018 figure custody HOLD. No original redraw claim.
packages.misconception: Do not assume electrostatic force remains constant if charge separation changes.

tasks.prediction: Does doubling tanθ necessarily double θ?
tasks.prompt: A charged pendulum bob of mass m is held at rest in a uniform horizontal electric field E. Its charge q is unchanged. On planet A the string angle from vertical is 30°. On planet B the same field and bob give 45°. Find g_B/g_A and explain whether tension is the same.

packages.title: Gravity and hydrostatic pressure
packages.lesson: In a stationary fluid with constant density, gauge pressure at depth h is ρgh. Derive by balancing a fluid column of area A: pressure difference times A equals ρAhg. Absolute pressure adds the surface pressure; comparisons must say which pressure is equal.

examples.prompt: Water ρ=1000 kg/m³, g=10, depth 2 m: gauge pressure.
Same fluid at g=5: depth for same gauge pressure.

packages.condition: Static liquid of constant density, uniform g; use gauge pressure unless absolute surface pressure is specified. Source identity remains preliminary.
packages.misconception: Depth is not the only variable; surface pressure may differ.

tasks.prediction: Can a shallower depth yield the same absolute pressure?
tasks.prompt: A probe in liquid A has density 1000 kg/m³, g=10 m/s², surface pressure 100 kPa and depth 4 m. Liquid B has density 2000 kg/m³, g=5 m/s² and surface pressure 120 kPa. Find depth B for the same absolute pressure; compare gauge pressures.
